extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and advanced law students studying US patent litigation and pleading practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and substantive rules on defenses, estoppel, pleading form, and notice requirements in U.S. patent litigation (historical statutes and case law illustrations). Focuses on which defenses are available, which require notice or special plea, and evidentiary effects of a patent grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel by consent decree / assignor estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant may be estopped by a decree by consent in a prior suit where he was defendant and the present plaintiff's assignor was plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example citation: United States Metallic Packing Co. v. Tripp (1887). The doctrine applies where prior consent decrees bear on the same subject matter and involve the assignor/assignee relationships; examine prior proceedings for consent decrees that could bind a party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee covenant not to deny validity / licensee estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee who has covenanted not to deny the validity of the patent or the licensor's title cannot defend against the patentability of the invention when sued by a rival bona fide patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the license includes an express covenant not to challenge validity or title, courts may bar the licensee from contesting patentability in suits by a rival bona fide patentee. However, nuances exist (e.g., privity, identity of parties); check whether the covenant's scope and the identity of the plaintiff permit an estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent applicant estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: One who has fraudulently endeavored to patent an invention is estopped from defending against a prior patent on the ground that the invention was then open to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Greenwood v. Bracher (1880) and related authority. If the applicant's conduct in procuring a patent is found fraudulent, he cannot later assert that prior public use/publication defeated an earlier patent—an equitable estoppel based on fraud may be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership without privity does not estop
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant who once owned an interest in a patent is not estopped to deny the validity of the patent if there is no privity of title between him and the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: Baltimore Car-Wheel Co. v. North Baltimore Passenger R.R. Co. (1884). Look for privity of title to determine whether an estoppel by prior ownership binds the present defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement not to manufacture does not estop absent conceded identity
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant agreeing not to manufacture a device is not estopped by that agreement to deny the patent's validity unless he has conceded that his device is identical in its essential characteristics with the patented device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Roemer v. Simon (1877). Parties who only promise not to practice their device retain the right to dispute that it is the same as the patented invention unless they have expressly conceded identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel by conduct and privity among multiple defendants
rubrics_metrics.description: An estoppel operating against one defendant does not bind other defendants unless they are in privity with him in reference to the subject-matter to which the estoppel appertains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When several defendants are sued, determine privity relationships before asserting an estoppel as to co-defendants. The treatise emphasizes that conduct-based estoppel is personal unless privity exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising/use may admit utility (evidentiary admission)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant who has used and advertised an invention as of great value thereby admits its utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See reference to Stanley v. Whipple and related authority. Public statements and advertising about an invention can be treated as admissions supporting utility in litigation; evaluate such conduct when assessing defenses that depend on lack of utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on using earlier patent to anticipate improvement (double-patenting defense)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant who infringes both the patent for the original and that for the improvement cannot set up the former as anticipating the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: Cantrell v. Wallick (1886), 117 U.S. 689. The rule prevents a separate earlier patent from serving as anticipation to invalidate a later patent covering an improvement in certain contexts; analyze relationship of claims (original vs improvement) carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each patent in suit may be separately attacked
rubrics_metrics.description: Where several patents constitute the basis of a single suit, each may be separately attacked by any of the methods of defence described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 965: Treat each asserted patent as separately defeasible; defendant may elect to attack some patents/claims and not others. Tactical implication: defenses can be tailored per-patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each claim may be defended as if a separate patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent which embraces several claims stands in this respect as if each claim were embodied in a separate patent; every claim is open to those defences which do not relate solely to the patent as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 965 and cases (e.g., Kelleher v. Darling). Evaluate infringement and validity at the claim level; some claims may be infringed while others not, and defenses may succeed as to particular claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissued and renewed-application patents subject to same objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Be-issued patents, and patents granted on renewed applications, may be met with the same objections as are admissible against original patents and patents granted on original applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reissued or renewed patents as vulnerable to the same categories of invalidity/defense (prior use, publication, insufficiency, fraud, etc.) as original patents; see concordant case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: General issue vs special plea/notice — foundational pleading rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Under common law the general issue was sufficient to cover all possible defences, but statutory changes (English and U.S. patent acts) introduced requirements of notice or special pleading for certain defenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical background: at common law 'not guilty' allowed all defenses; 5 & 6 W. IV. and later U.S. acts required notices or special pleas for particular defenses. When advising litigants, determine whether statute or rule demands notice or a special plea for the intended defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent and specification as prima facie evidence (Act of 1790)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act of 1790 provided that the patent and specification shall be prima facie evidence that the patentee was the true and first inventor and that the description given was correct; but a defendant might, upon due notice, offer evidence that the specification concealed part of the invention or added more than necessary so as to mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this framework, attacks on the sufficiency/concealment in the specification required prior notice to the patentee; other defenses could be raised under general issue. Use this rule when analyzing older cases or tracing the evolution of burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three necessary conditions for patent validity
rubrics_metrics.description: To the validity of a patent three things were necessary: (1) the invention should be patentable; (2) the patentee should be its first and true inventor; (3) he should place his invention fully within the knowledge of the public (sufficient disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise highlights the different character of these elements: the first two are fixed historical facts; the third (sufficiency of disclosure) involves human judgment and testing by skilled artisans. The treatment of evidence and notice differs among these elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary effect and burden shifting under successive patent acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory changes altered burdens: the Act of 1790 made patents prima facie evidence (shifting burden); the Act of 1793 omitted that presumption and required patentee oath; subsequent acts (1836, 1870) modified which defenses required notice and restored some presumptions and notice rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When citing precedents or construing historical decisions, pay attention to which statute governed the case because it controls whether the patent was prima facie evidence and which defenses required prior notice or special plea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defences requiring prior notice under the Act of 1793 (grounds of repeal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Act of 1793 the defences requiring prior notice (and which could render the patent void) were: fraudulent specification; prior use; prior publication; and a surreptitious patent obtained for another person's discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These grounds were treated as fatal defects that could justify repeal of a patent. Notice (e.g., thirty days before trial) was required to admit evidence on these matters. Counsel must serve the required notice before offering such evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defences requiring prior notice under the Act of 1836
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Act of 1836 the defenses of which notice was required included: a fraudulent specification; prior invention by another than the patentee; prior publication; abandonment by public use or sale; a surreptitious patent obtained for the invention of another; and failure of an alien patentee to put his invention on the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The act of 1836 reintroduced the general issue but kept notice as a condition precedent to offering evidence on these specific topics. Practitioners must ensure compliance with notice requirements for these categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice is not a pleading but may be replaced by a special plea
rubrics_metrics.description: The required notice of special matter is not a plea and is not part of the record; a special plea serving the same function (completeness of statement, time and mode of service) may be substituted for the notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court practice permits filing a special plea instead of serving a separate notice, but the plea must effectively perform the notice's warning function. Failure to provide adequate notice/plea can preclude admission of evidence on those defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale for requiring notice for insufficiency of specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A requirement of notice for attacks on the sufficiency of the specification is justified because sufficiency cannot be known until the specification is published and tried by skilled artisans; it would be unfair to require the patentee to keep evidence ready at all times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explains that insufficiency is a matter of human judgment and experience; hence the defendant must notify the patentee to allow preparation. This rationale underpins historical notice rules and affects fairness-based procedural analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical effect of pleading/notice rules in modern practice (as described)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where statutes (e.g., Act of 1870/Rev. Stat.) permit the general issue and require notice for certain matters, the correct interpretation is that the general issue remains broad but evidence on specified topics is conditional on prior notice; the notice limits the defendant's right to introduce certain evidence, not his right to plead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the approach that preserves the general-issue breadth while enforcing statutory notice requirements. Courts have consistently interpreted modern statutes to mean notice is a condition precedent for admission of evidence on enumerated defenses rather than a bar to pleading them.
